## Methods

Identification of AACRN(L) proteins in organisms
BLASTP and TBLASTN searches were conducted on the NCBI database (https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Blast.cgi), and target sequences with e-values above 10−10 and proteins with unrelated domain were discarded. These target sequences were used to perform iterative-BLAST to find more AACRN(L) proteins in eumycota and animalia.

Alignment, phylogenetic, and synteny analysis
Protein and DNA sequences were aligned by MUSCLE software (v3.8.31) for its high accuracy and speed, and Jalview software (v2.10) is used for visualizing comparison results. Maximum likelihood (ML) phylogenetic trees were generated using MEGA7, with WAG+G model and 1000 bootstrap replicates. Neighbor-Joining (NJ) trees were generated using MEGA7, with JTT model and 1000 bootstrap replicates. ITOL website (https://itol.embl.de/) were used to beautify the above phylogenetic tree. For gene synteny analysis, AACRNL genes were used as focal reference gene to TBLASTN the genome of seven indicated fish (S. Formosus, M. miiuy, P. platessa, O. latipes, O. niloticus, A. alosa, and D. rerio).

Domain, tertiary structure, and molecular docking analysis
The protein domain structure was predicted by the SMART website (http://smart.embl-heidelberg.de/). The tertiary structure of AACRNL proteins were predicted by AlphaFold Server (https://golgi.sandbox.google.com/). The molecular docking between mART domains and NAD+ were performed by AlphaFold Server website (AlphaFold Server (google.com)) and PyMOL software.

Identification of transposable elements flanking the AACRNL gene
To investigate the replicative transposition mechanism of AACRNL, ~5 kb of genomic DNA flanking the AACRNL gene was extracted. Then we used the BLAST tool at FishTEDB (https://www.fishtedb.com/) and Dfam website (https://dfam.org/search/sequence) to analyze potential transposon components.

Fish and challenge
M. miiuy (~50 g) was obtained from Zhoushan Fisheries Research Institute, Zhejiang Province, China. Fish was acclimated in aerated seawater tanks at 25°C for 6 weeks before experiments. In the SCRV injection group, fish was challenged with 200 μl SCRV at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 5 through intraperitoneal. As a comparison, 200 μl of physiological saline was used to challenge the individuals. Afterwards, the fish were sacrificed at different time points, and kidney and spleen tissues were collected for RNA extraction. SCRV virus was isolated as described previously39.

Cell culture
M. miiuy kidney cells (MKCs) were cultured in L-15 medium (HyClone) supplemented with 15% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Gibco), 100 U/ml penicillin, and 100 μg/ml streptomycin at 26°C. MKC cells were prepared from the kidney of M. miiuy as previously described40. EPC cells (ATCC, RRID: CVCL_4361) were maintained in medium 199 (HyClone) supplemented with 10% FBS (Gibco), 2 mM of L-glutamine, 100 U/mL of penicillin, and 100 mg/mL of streptomycin under humidified conditions at 26°C with 5% CO2. HEK293T cells (ATCC, RRID: CVCL_0063) were cultured in DMEM (HyClone) supplemented with 10% FBS, 100 U/ml penicillin, and 100 mg/ml streptomycin at 37°C in 5% CO2. All cells were tested negative for mycoplasma contamination and morphologically confirmed. No cell line was used for more than 20 passages after thawing from frozen stocks.

Cells transfection
Cells were transiently transfected with siRNA in 24-well plates using Lipofectamine RNAiMAX (Invitrogen) and with DNA plasmids using Lipofectamine 3000 (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. For functional analyses, the overexpression plasmid (500 ng per well) and siRNA (100 nM) were transfected into cells in a culture medium and then harvested for further detection.

RNA interference
The AACRNLβ-specific small interfering RNA (siRNA; si-AACRNLβ-1 and si-AACRNLβ-2) sequences were 5′-GGAUGUUUCAACAAGAUCATT-3′ and 5′-GGACUUCUGUUGAAAGAAATT-3′, respectively. The TRAF6-specific small interfering RNA (si-TRAF6) is as follows: 5′-ACACCAUGCAAGGAGCUUUTT-3′. The scrambled control RNA sequences were 5′-UUCUCCGAACGUGUCACGUTT-3′.

Plasmids construction
The full-length coding sequence (CDS) of expression proteins of miiuy croaker (M. miiuy) were generated by PCR and cloned into pcDNA3.1 (Invitrogen) with specific tags. HA-tagged wild-type ubiquitin (UB-HA) and HA-tagged ubiquitin mutant expression plasmids were constructed with the template of pRK5-HA-ubiquitin-WT (Addgene, Cat# 17608) using ClonExpress II One Step Cloning Kit (Vazyme). Site or deletion mutants of AACRNLβ and TRAF6 were amplified by PCR with specific primers based on the recombinant plasmid. For protein purification, expression plasmids with 8× His tag was constructed based on pcDNA3.1. The correct construction of the recombinant plasmids was verified through Sanger sequencing and extracted using an Endotoxin-Free Plasmid DNA Miniprep Kit (Tiangen, China). The primers are listed in Supplementary Data 1.

Cell viability
Cell viability was assessed 48 h post-transfection in MKCs using the Cell-Titer-Glo luminescent assay (Promega), following the manufacturer’s protocol.

Protein purification and analysis
(His8)-tagged expression plasmids of M. miiuy were transiently overexpressed in 293T cells and lysed in a binding buffer (500 mM NaCl, 20 mM Tris/HCl [pH 7.4], 20 mM Imidazole, and 1% Triton X-100) including protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche). The lysate was incubated overnight at 4°C with anti-His beads (Solarbio). Anti-His beads were washed subsequently with washing buffer (500 mM NaCl, 20 mM Tris/HCl [pH 7.4], 20 mM Imidazole, and 1% Triton X-100). Proteins were eluted by addition of elution buffer (500 mM NaCl, 20 mM Tris/HCl [pH 7.4], 500 mM Imidazole, and 1% Triton X-100) to the beads. The purity of recombinant proteins was determined by SDS-PAGE separation or ponceau S. The purified AACRNLβ and AACRNLβ-HYY proteins were used to perform in vitro ADP-ribosylation assays.

RNA extraction and quantitative real-time PCR
The TRIzol Reagent (Invitrogen) was utilized for total RNA extraction, and subsequent cDNA synthesis was performed using the FastQuant RT Kit (Tiangen). The expression profiles of each gene were conducted by using the SYBR Premix Ex Taq™ (Takara). Quantitative real-time PCR was carried out using an Applied Biosystems® QuantStudio 3 (Thermo Fisher Scientific). β-actin served as the internal control for mRNA. The primer sequences are detailed in Supplementary Data 1.

Western blotting
Cellular lysates were prepared using 1× SDS-PAGE loading buffer. Protein extraction from cells was conducted, and quantification was performed using the BCA Protein Assay kit (Vazyme). The proteins were separated by SDS-PAGE (10%) and transferred onto PVDF membranes using a semidry blotting technique (Bio-Rad Trans Blot Turbo System). The membranes were then blocked with 5% BSA and probed with various antibodies. The antibody against AACRNLβ was diluted at 1:1000 (Customized in Genscript); The antibody against TRAF6 was diluted at 1: 500 (Boster, A00185); The antibody against IκBα was diluted at 1:500 (absin, abs106057); The antibody against TNF-α was diluted at 1:500 (ABclonal); The antibody against H3K27me3 (Beyotime, AF5710), H3K9me3 (Beyotime, AF5707), H3 (Beyotime, AF7101), and EZH2 (Beyotime, AF6828) were diluted at 1:500 (Beyotime); anti-Flag (Beyotime, AF519), anti-Myc (Beyotime, AF2864), anti-HA (Beyotime, AH158) and anti-Tubulin (Beyotime, AT819) monoclonal antibodies were diluted at 1: 1000; and HRP-conjugated anti-rabbit IgG (Abbkine, A25022) or anti-mouse IgG (Abbkine, A25012) at 1:5000. The immunoreactive proteins were visualized using Western Bright TM ECL (Advansta), and digital imaging was conducted with a cold CCD camera.

Co-immunoprecipitation
The cells were lysed in the cold IP buffer. The supernatant from cell lysates was incubated with indicated antibodies. Then, the protein A/G beads were incubated with the lysates overnight at 4°C. The beads were washed three times with cold lysis buffer and resuspended in the protein loading buffer. The immunoprecipitates and whole-cell lysates were followed by western blotting analysis.

Ni2+-NTA pull-down assay
Ni2+-NTA pull-down assay was done as described previously41. Cells cultured in 10-cm plates were transfected with the indicated plasmids. Cells from each plate were washed and collected with ice-cold PBS and divided into two aliquots. One sample was lysed with NP-40 lysis buffer and analyzed by immunoblotting directly to examine the expression of indicated proteins. Another sample was lysed in buffer A (8 M urea, 50 mM NaHPO4.H2O, 300 mM NaCl, 10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 10 mM imidazole) and subjected to sonication for 20 s. Cell lysates were incubated with 50-µL pre-equilibrated Ni2+-NTA beads (denaturation type) for 8 h at 4°C. Then, beads were washed four times sequentially with buffer A and B (same as A except with 20 mM imidazole). Beads bound with His-tagged proteins were boiled with 2× SDS loading buffer containing 200 mM imidazole and were subjected to immunoblot.

Immunofluorescence
Cells cultured on glass coverslips in 24-well plates were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min following a triple wash with PBS. The cells were permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100 in PBS (PBST) for 15 min. After a 60-min block with 5% BSA, the cells were subjected to a 10-h incubation with the primary antibody at 4°C. Following three washes with PBS, the cells were exposed to a fluorescent-dye conjugated secondary antibody for 60 min at room temperature. Post a 10-min DAPI counterstain, the fluorescence signals of the cells were captured using a Leica fluorescence microscope.

In vitro ADP-ribosylation assay
After obtaining the purified proteins, ADP-ribosylation assays were carried out in 30-ml reaction buffer (50 mM Tris, pH 8.0, 0.2 mM DTT, 4 mM MgCl2) with 100 mM NAD+ (Macklin, N814818) or 100 mM Bio-NAD+ (Mreda, M256875) for 45 min at room temperature. The reactions were stopped by addition of SDS sample buffer, and the products were probed with mono-ADP-Ribose antibody (BIO-RAD, AbD33204) or streptavidin–HRP (Beyotime, A0303).

In vivo ADP-ribosylation analysis
MKC cells were transfected with AACRNLβ-Myc or AACRNLβ-HYY-Myc plasmids, then cell lysate was immunoprecipitated by Myc antibody and the interacted proteins with mono-ADPr modification were immunoblotted with mono-ADPr antibody to analyse the ADP-ribosylation effects of AACRNLβ in vivo. To detect whether TRAF6 and EZH2 have mono-ADPr modification in vivo, MKC cell lysate was immunoprecipitated by IgG antibody or mono-ADP-Ribose antibody, then TRAF6 and EZH2 antibody were used to detect mono-ADP-ribosylation.

Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay
MKC cells were seeded in 10 cm² dishes and transfected with plasmids once the cell density reached 5.0 × 10⁶. For chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP), cells were cross-linked with 1% formaldehyde at 37°C for 10 min, then quenched with glycine for 5 min at room temperature. After two washes with PBS, cells were lysed on ice, collected, and sonicated to shear chromatin. Lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 12,000 rpm (~13,800 × g) for 10 min at 4°C. The resulting supernatant was incubated with the appropriate antibody overnight at 4°C with rotation. Protein A/G agarose beads were added and incubated for 2 h at 4°C. After centrifugation at 6000 rpm (~3500 × g) for 5 min, the supernatant was discarded. Beads were sequentially washed with low-salt wash buffer (twice), LiCl wash buffer, and TE buffer. Immunocomplexes were eluted with elution buffer and diluted to 500 ml using diffusion buffer. Cross-links were reversed by adding 5 M NaCl and incubating at 65°C for 12 h, followed by treatment with 0.5 M EDTA, 1 M Tris-HCl, and 20 mg/ml Proteinase K at 45°C for 2 h.

Statistical analysis
Statistical analyses were performed using Prism v8 (GraphPad Software). Data are expressed as the mean ± SE from at least three independent experiments, each performed with three technical replicates. Comparisons between two groups were performed using a two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test. For comparisons involving more than two groups, one-way ANOVA followed by Duncan’s post-hoc multiple comparison test was conducted. The relative gene expression data was acquired using the 2−ΔΔCT method42. Effect sizes (Cohen’s d for t-tests and η² for ANOVA) were calculated within Prism v8. A value of p < 0.05 was considered significant.

Ethics statement
All animal experimental procedures were performed in accordance with the National Institutes of Health’s Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals, and the experimental protocols were approved by the Research Ethics Committee of Shanghai Ocean University (No. SHOU-DW-2025-033).

### Reviewer 1

In this manuscript, the discovery of a ‘selfish’ gene product that is endemic to a variety of organisms within multiple phyla is reported. The authors describe AACRN as a Crinkler family protein product encoded in host genomes that resembles pathogenic gene products. In this manuscript the authors describe the distribution and frequency of AACRN genes in a number of kingdoms and phyla. The authors go on to characterize the genetic structure of AACRN families and conclude that beta and gamma members in fish species are preferentially replicating themselves within their hosts genome. They elucidate that AACRN is often within a non-autonomously replicating transposon and that AACRN is able to interact with EZH2 to inhibit histone methylation of the transposon and thereby increase their expression and subsequent ability to propagate with the transposon. Given that these types of pathogenic gene products and transposition mechanisms activate host immune mechanisms the authors investigated how AACRN manipulates host defense mechanisms. To this end they describe how AACRN can ADP ribosylate TRAF6 and target it for ubiquitylation and degradation.
Overall, this is a well written and intriguing body of work describing a novel form of selfish gene or pathogenic gene product that has persisted in host genomes. The data are of high quality and the experiments, their interpretation, and conclusions are well reasoned and appropriate. I have a few suggests of places to improve the manuscript before publication. They are ranked roughly in order of importance for improving the manuscript.
1) The authors conclude that AACRN is strictly a remnant of pathogenesis and its perpetuation is an example of a gene product that is functionless to the host but who’s mechanism of action and gene structure ensures propagation. It struck me that many examples of repetitive elements in mammals are described as junk or remnants of ancient infections until they are discovered to have an endogenous function. The authors discuss examples of this (eg RAG proteins) but conclude AACRN is just a pathogen. I think this conclusion is premature. There is no investigation of how this gene could have an endogenous function that is beneficial to their host fish species. This issue is potentially addressable. Morpholino knock downs are routine in zebrafish embryos and the authors indicate that Danio rario has an AACRN gamma family of genes. If knock down compromised development then the host has exapted AACRN function. Without an experiment such as this to address the hosts relationship with AACRN I think it is premature to discuss it as purely a pathogen and the discussion should instead indicate that this is an open question.
2) My biggest criticism of the data as presented is the lack of investigation of endogenous AACRN. Much of the transfection based approaches to investigate ubiquitination and ribosylation make sense to me, but the data that implicates endogenous AACRN in these types of activities is lacking. Does endogenous AACRN bind to TRAF6? The siRNA knock down of AACRN in Fig. 5G is not the most convincing with regards to TRAF6 levels being dependent on AACRN expression. Similarly, showing endogenous stabilization of AACRN by MG132 instead of transfection in Fig. 6A is key to validating the more artificial and transfection based experiments that ensue. However the methods and figure legends allude to the occasional use of 293T cells and the difficulty of finding those experiments more clearly is troubling. It would be better if these specific experiments (ie. panels within figures) were specifically indicated in the results narrative so they can be readily seen as heterologous.

Many figures are a full page in landscape mode. Figure 1 exemplifies this as in addition to occupying this much space it’s panels are extensively text dependent and already too small to read. You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
  1. The revised paper
  2. Your original Round 1 review
  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

Crinkler effectors are iconic toxins deployed by pathogens to suppress host immunity, a function long thought exclusive to pathogenic species. Here, we uncover a striking evolutionary twist: an ADP-ribosyltransferase-associated Crinkler-like protein that has repurposed its toxin-derived activity to function as an epigenetic parasite in free-living eukaryotes, challenging the paradigm that Crinkler effectors are exclusively pathogen-restricted virulence factors. The ADP-ribosyltransferase-associated Crinkler-like protein retains a functional mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase domain homologous to diphtheria toxin, yet exhibits degeneration of N-terminal host-targeting domain, severing ties to canonical pathogenic functions. This activity enables dual subversion of host mechanisms: the ADP-ribosyltransferase-associated Crinkler-like protein mono-ADP-ribosylates the EZH2, reducing H3K27me3-mediated silencing and reactivating its own locus and adjacent transposons to drive replicative amplification; simultaneously, it modifies the immune adaptor TRAF6, suppressing NF-κB and IRF3 pathways to weaken innate immune surveillance and facilitate sustained propagation within the host genome. Notably, this parasitic strategy is countered by host detoxification: TRAF6 ubiquitinates ADP-ribosyltransferase-associated Crinkler-like protein, targeting it for proteasomal degradation. Together, our findings reveal how a toxin-derived effector escaped pathogenic contexts to evolve as a selfish genomic element, leveraging toxin-like activity to subvert epigenetic and immune barriers and redefining the evolutionary potential of Crinkler toxins as drivers of genomic conflict beyond pathogenicity.

---

## Introduction

Pathogenic microbes rely on secreted effector proteins to commandeer host cells and facilitate infection1,2. These virulence factors can disable immune defenses, hijack signaling pathways, and reprogram host physiology to the pathogen’s advantage1,2. In Gram-negative bacteria, type III secretion system effectors are renowned for targeting mitochondria and other organelles to control host cell death and inflammation3. Among oomycetes and fungi, Crinkler (CRN) proteins constitute a prominent effector family that exemplifies the complexity of host manipulation strategies4. First discovered in the potato late blight pathogen Phytophthora infestans, certain CRNs induced a characteristic leaf “crinkling and necrosis” phenotype when expressed in plants, highlighting their virulence potential5.

Structurally, canonical CRN effectors exhibit a modular architecture comprising conserved N-terminal and C-terminal domains that underpin their functional versatility6. The N-terminal domain, ~130 amino acids in length, includes the LXLFLAK motif, ubiquitin-like (UBL) folds, and α-helical structures responsible for host cell translocation4,7. The C-terminal region of CRN encompasses several effector functionalities, including restriction endonuclease (REase), protein kinase, HNH endonuclease, LK nuclease (a RNase), and multiple distinct peptidase domains, predicted to carry their toxicity determinants4,6,8,9. This modularity is thought to enable CRNs to diversify rapidly in response to selective pressures, fueling pathogen adaptation during host-pathogen coevolution.

Unexpectedly, recent comparative genomics surveys have uncovered CRN homologues across multiple free-living eukaryotic lineages, including chlorophyte algae, land plants, amoebozoans, and animals, challenging the long-held notion that these effectors are exclusive to pathogenic taxa7. This unexpected distribution raises fundamental questions about their evolutionary persistence: why do such virulence-associated genes remain embedded in the genomes of non-pathogenic organisms, and what functions, if any, do they perform outside classical pathogenic contexts? Addressing these questions is essential to expanding our understanding of effector evolution and function beyond classical pathogen-host paradigms.

Effector genes often reside within dynamic genomic contexts shaped by transposable elements and mobile genetic elements that facilitate their mobilization and diversification in pathogens10. Such genes are typically subject to strong positive selection because their toxin functions confer clear fitness benefits during infection, facilitating immune suppression and colonization11. By contrast, free-living non-pathogenic eukaryotes are ecologically isolated, limiting horizontal gene transfer opportunities through plasmids, viruses, or symbiotic interactions, which constrains the spread of virulence-associated genes. Furthermore, these sequences are often targets of host epigenetic repression mechanisms—such as H3K27me3-mediated chromatin silencing and DNA methylation—that restrict expression and genomic propagation of potentially invasive elements12,13. These constraints have reinforced the paradigm that effectors are confined to pathogenic contexts and rendered their evolutionary persistence in nonpathogenic genomes largely enigmatic.

Here, we report the discovery and functional characterization of a CRN homologue, ADP-ribosyltransferase-associated CRN-like (AACRNL), whose homologues are broadly distributed across free-living eukaryotic lineages. Unlike canonical CRNs, AACRNL have retained functional toxin-like enzymatic module but exhibit degeneration of N-terminal targeting domain, uncoupling them from classical host translocation. Remarkably, AACRNL co-opts its ART activity to mono-ADP-ribosylate EZH2, eroding H3K27me3-dependent repression and enabling the activation and replication of its own locus and adjacent transposons. Concurrently, AACRNL modifies TRAF6 to suppress NF-κB/IRF3 signaling, creating an immunologically permissive environment for its expansion. This dual strategy reveals how a virulence-derived effector can be repurposed as an epigenetic parasite in free-living eukaryotes, challenging conventional views of CRN biology and illuminating broader principles of genome conflict and adaptation.

---

## Results

Distribution and degeneration of AACRN(L) in free-living eukaryotes
The canonical CRN effector consists of an N-terminal domain responsible for host targeting and a toxin-related C-terminal domain (Fig. 1a). Based on this modular architecture, we identified a distinct type of CRN effectors, termed AACRN, characterized by an N-terminal UBL domain and a C-terminal ADP-ribosyltransferase (ART) domain (Fig. 1b). In addition, we identified a related variant in which the UBL domain has undergone extensive degeneration; we refer to this lineage as AACRN-Like (AACRNL) (Fig. 1b). Although AACRN effectors are typically associated with pathogenic functions, AACRN(L) homologs are also present in several free-living eukaryotes. Specifically, comprehensive search across multiple phyla revealed that the AACRN(L) family were detected in free-living eukaryotes like Porifera, Cnidaria, Echinodermata, Chordata, Rotifera, Nematora, and Arthropoda of animalia (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Fig. 1). Notably, the occurrence of AACRN(L) genes is limited to a minority of taxa and can vary considerably even within the same phylum. For example, within Chordata, the AACRNL family was identified exclusively in Actinopteri, a class of bony fish, which is also the highest living organism distributed by the AACRNL family (Fig. 1c). Given that the N-terminal domain is critical for host targeting, we examined its integrity in these free-living organisms. We observed pronounced degeneration of the N-terminal regions in AACRN effectors. For instance, the AACRNL homologues from Acipenser ruthenus and Porites lobata, the UBL domain has degenerated and lost the essential RGG motif required for ubiquitin chain formation (Fig. 1d, e). Overall, these findings demonstrate that AACRNL homologues persist in the genomes of certain free-living eukaryotes, and their N-terminal domain responsible for host targeting has also degraded, which may reflect a potential functional shift.

AACRNL exerts toxicity in free-living organisms through its ADP-ribosyltransferase activity
To identify the key residues responsible for the ADP-ribosyltransferase activity of AACRN(L), we collected AACRN(L) protein sequences from different phyla, along with two well-characterized bacterial toxins with mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase (mART) activity: diphtheria toxin from Corynebacterium diphtheriae and exotoxin A from Pseudomonas aeruginosa14. Sequence alignment of the mART domain revealed a conserved H-Y-Y motif (Fig. 2a), which is essential for NAD⁺ co-substrate binding15. Next, we extracted the structural domain sequences of Miichthys miiuy AACRNL and C. diphtheriae diphtheria toxin, performing molecular docking with NAD+. The results showed that in both AACRNL and diphtheria toxin, both the “H” and the “Y” residues had interatomic contacts with NAD+ (Fig. 2b). To validate the functional importance of this motif, we generated point mutations in the H-Y-Y motif of M. miiuy AACRNL (Fig. 2c). AACRNL efficiently co-precipitated mono-ADP-ribosylation (mono-ADPr) from cell lysates, but AACRNL-HYY mutants did not (Fig. 2d). Additionally, self-modifying activity tests showed that AACRNL, but not AACRNL-HYY, was modified by mono-ADP-ribose (Fig. 2e). Furthermore, when purified AACRNL or AACRNL-HYY proteins were incubated with biotin-labeled NAD+, only AACRNL’s auto-modification was detected by streptavidin-HRP on western blots (Fig. 2f). Considering the structural homology between AACRNL and diphtheria toxin, as well as the origin of its toxin effector domain, we further investigated whether AACRNL functions as a toxin in fish, the highest-order lineage where AACRNL is distributed. Indeed, we found that AACRNL exerts mART-dependent inhibition of cellular viability (Fig. 2g). In addition, AACRNL suppressed the IRF3 and NF-κB pathways and downregulated the expression of antiviral and pro-inflammatory factors (Fig. 2h–k). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that AACRNL possesses robust mART activity and retains toxin-like functions even in free-living eukaryotes.

AACRNL replicates in teleost via adjacent transposable elements
We further assessed the distribution and abundance of AACRNL genes in teleost, the highest-level vertebrate group in which AACRNL homologs have been identified so far. AACRNL exhibits lineage-specific expansion and contraction in bony fish, with Cyprinus carpio displaying the highest number of AACRNL copies, although their transcriptional activity is yet to be elucidated (Fig. 3a). In contrast, Takifugu rubripes is the only bony fish lacking AACRNL (Fig. 3a). Through a comprehensive analysis of chromosome-level whole genome data from seven fish species (Scleropages Formosus, M. miiuy, Pleuronectes platessa, Oryzias latipes, Oreochromis niloticus, Alosa alosa, and Danio rerio), we found that phylogenetic analysis of AACRNLs from these fish species revealed significant clustering into three lineages, which we refer to as AACRNLα, AACRNLβ, and AACRNLγ (Fig. 3b). The linear relationship around the AACRNLα gene is relatively conservative and single copy, indicating that it has lost its replication ability (Fig. 3b, c). However, AACRNLβ and AACRNLγ exhibit a very limited linear relationship and multiple copies, indicating that they have undergone replication (Fig. 3b, c).

To investigate the replication mechanisms of AACRNLβ and AACRNLγ, we examined their surrounding genomic sequences. Among the three copies identified in M. miiuy, AACRNLα was unable to transpose, while the other two included AACRNLβ and another copy that had become inactive, which we designated pAACRNLβ (Fig. 3c). Based on their linear arrangement, the right flank of pAACRNLβ was identical to that of AACRNLβ, both containing the hce1 and lce1 genes, indicating that pAACRNLβ originated from the duplication of AACRNLβ (Fig. 3d). Notably, we observed terminal inverted repeats (TIRs) of a non-autonomous hAT_Charlie transposable element flanking both sides of the AACRNLβ and lce1 loci, suggesting that the replication and transposition of AACRNLβ may have been mediated by the hAT_Charlie (Fig. 3d). We also found that autonomous mariner transposon elements are present on both sides of the AACRNLβ1 and AACRNLβ3 genes in P. platessa. Upstream of AACRNLβ1, there is the gtse1 gene, and within the last intron, the 5′ TIR and transposase of an autonomous mariner transposon are present. At the 3′ flanking region of AACRNLβ3, the 3′ TIR of an autonomous mariner transposon is detected. Analysis of the flanking regions of the AACRNLβ4, AACRNLβ5, and AACRNLβ6 genes in P. platessa also revealed autonomous mariner transposon elements together with the last exon of gtse1, confirming that these genes indeed originated through transpositional duplication from AACRNLβ1, AACRNLβ3, and related loci (Fig. 3e). Similarly, TIR sequences of non-autonomous hAT transposons were also detected flanking the AACRNLγ1 locus in zebrafish, further supporting our hypothesis (Fig. 3f). In summary, our research found that AACRNL can rely on neighboring transposable elements for selfish propagation in teleost genomes.

AACRNLβ abrogates H3K27me3-dependent repression of its locus and flanking hAT elements
Given that transposable elements in the host genome are generally maintained in a silenced state, yet replicative transposition of AACRNL is remarkably prevalent, this suggests that AACRNL may possess the capacity to activate these elements. Sequence alignment of the conserved “HGT” motif, which is essential for mART activity15, revealed that AACRNLα has lost this enzymatic function, whereas AACRNLβ and AACRNLγ retain intact catalytic domains (Fig. 4a). Consistent with their mobility, AACRNLα was unable to undergo replication, whereas AACRNLβ and AACRNLγ exhibited active transposition (Fig. 3b–f). These observations suggested that the intrinsic mART activity of AACRNL might be required for its selfish propagation (Fig. 4a). H3K27me3 and H3K9me3 are key chromatin modifications that silence transposable elements and repress gene transcription16. We found that M. miiuy AACRNLα, which lacks mART activity, was unable to suppress H3K27me3 levels, whereas AACRNLβ effectively reduced this repressive mark (Fig. 4b). Consistently, the AACRNLβ-HYY mutant, which has lost mART activity, also failed to inhibit H3K27me3 deposition (Fig. 4c). Given that H3K27me3 is deposited by the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2), we examined whether AACRNLβ interacts with PRC2 components. Co-immunoprecipitation experiments revealed that AACRNLβ specifically associated with EZH2, the catalytic subunit of PRC2, but not with SUZ12 (Fig. 4d). Moreover, immunoblotting with mono-ADP-ribose–specific antibodies confirmed in vivo mono-ADP-ribosylation of EZH2 (Fig. 4e). In vitro assays further demonstrated that AACRNLβ directly mediates mono-ADP-ribosylation of EZH2 (Fig. 4f, g). Beyond modifying EZH2, AACRNLβ also promotes the degradation of EZH2 protein in an enzymatic activity–dependent manner, without affecting ezh2 mRNA levels (Fig. 4h–j). Therefore, AACRNLβ can suppress H3K27me3 modification levels by inhibiting EZH2.

To determine whether AACRNLβ-driven reduction of H3K27me3 could relieve silencing at its own locus and neighboring hAT elements, we designed four pairs of ChIP-qPCR primers spanning the region from the AACRNLβ promoter to the 5′ TIR (Fig. 4k). Chromatin immunoprecipitation revealed that both AACRNLβ and the adjacent hAT sequences were enriched in H3K27me3 marks (Fig. 4l). Overexpression of EZH2 further increased H3K27me3 deposition, whereas co-transfection of wild-type AACRNLβ, but not the catalytically inactive mutant, effectively abrogated EZH2-mediated enrichment at these loci (Fig. 4m). Functionally, EZH2 suppressed AACRNLβ mRNA expression and decreased the recruitment of POLR2A, a core subunit of RNA polymerase II, to the AACRNLβ promoter (Fig. 4n, o). In contrast, co-transfection of AACRNLβ reversed this repression, suggesting that AACRNLβ is capable of self-activation (Fig. 4o). Consistently, siRNA knockdown of AACRN reduced POLR2A binding at its promoter (Fig. 4p). Collectively, these results demonstrate that AACRNLβ relieves H3K27me3-mediated silencing at its locus and neighboring hAT elements by targeting and modifying EZH2. This establishes a permissive chromatin environment that facilitates both self-activation and replicative transposition, thereby linking AACRNL’s mART enzymatic activity to its capacity for selfish genomic spread.

Viral infection triggers AACRNL activation and subsequent genomic instability
To investigate the activation dynamics and functional consequences of AACRNL, we analyzed its expression during zebrafish embryogenesis to capture baseline developmental activity, and upon viral infection to assess stress-induced activation. Single-cell analysis across early (4–6 h), mid (8–12 h), and late (24 h) embryonic stages showed that all five AACRNLγ members were transcriptionally silent, with AACRNLγ2, γ3, and γ5 loci enriched for H3K27me3, indicative of developmental repression (Fig. 5a). Notably, this silencing was reversible: SVCV infection strongly induced AACRNLγ2, γ3, and γ5, whereas γ1 and γ4 remained undetectable, suggesting potential loss of transcriptional competence in these loci (Fig. 5b). Similarly, M. miiuy AACRNLβ was markedly upregulated upon SCRV infection, as shown by RNA-seq and validated by qPCR in spleen, kidney, and MKC cells (Fig. 5c–f). Functional assays demonstrated that siRNA-mediated knockdown of AACRNLβ restored H3K27me3 levels suppressed by viral infection and prevented DNA damage, as indicated by tp53, p21, and gadd45a induction, revealing that infection-induced AACRNLβ promotes genomic instability (Fig. 5g, h). This function required AACRNLβ’s mART activity (Fig. 5i). Finally, wild-type AACRNLβ, but not the catalytically inactive AACRNLβ-HYY mutant, significantly increased the expression of transposon RNAs known to respond to pathogen challenge, including LINEs and ERVs (Fig. 5j). These findings indicate that pathogen-induced AACRNL activation promotes DNA damage and creates a permissive chromatin environment for transposon expression.

AACRNLβ mono-ADP-ribosylates TRAF6
Given that transposon activity and exogenous genetic elements often trigger host immune surveillance, we investigate how AACRNLβ creates an immune permissive environment to promote selfish reproduction. Co-immunoprecipitation results showed that AACRNLβ specifically binds to TRAF6, not to TRAF3, TBK1, TAK1, or NEMO proteins (Fig. 6a). Immunofluorescence revealed that AACRNLβ is in both the cytoplasm and nucleus, while TRAF6 is in the cytoplasm (Fig. 6b). Endogenous co-IP demonstrated that TRAF6 specifically interacts with AACRNLβ, and AACRNLβ and its mutants interact with TRAF6 with the same binding affinity (Fig. 6c, d). Mono-ADPr antibodies confirmed that TRAF6 undergoes mono-ribosylation in vivo (Fig. 6e), and AACRNLβ can mediate TRAF6 mono-ribosylation in vitro (Fig. 6f, g). To identify deribosylases that reverse this modification, we examined TRAF6-interacting proteins in our mass spectrometry data and discovered ARH3, a poly-ADP ribose glycohydrolase17,18. In addition, we also constructed a Macro-3 domain plasmid from the ARTD8 protein of M. miiuy responsible for specifically removing mono-ribosylation modifications18. His-pulldown results indicated that both ARH3 and Macro3 can interact with TRAF6 (Fig. 6h). Overexpression of AACRNLβ significantly promoted the binding of Macro3, but not ARH3, to TRAF6, while catalytically inactive AACRNLβ-HYY did not affect their interaction (Fig. 6i, j). These findings strongly support that AACRNLβ induces TRAF6 mono-ADP-ribosylation19.

AACRNLβ inhibits TRAF6-mediated ubiquitin signaling
To define how AACRNLβ-mediated mono-ADP-ribosylation affects TRAF6 function, we first examined its impact on TRAF6 stability. Knockdown or overexpression of AACRNLβ increased or decreased TRAF6 protein levels without affecting TRAF6 mRNA levels (Fig. 7a, b). During SCRV or V. anguillarum infection, AACRNLβ consistently suppressed TRAF6 protein expression (Fig. 7c). The AACRNLβ-HYY mutant also significantly degraded TRAF6, though less effectively (Fig. 7d). Cycloheximide (CHX) assays confirmed that AACRNLβ shortened the half-life of endogenous TRAF6 protein (Fig. 7e). To determine if AACRNLβ-mediated TRAF6 degradation was dependent on ubiquitin-proteasome, autophagosome, or lysosomal pathways, MKC cells were treated with MG132, 3-Methyladenine (3-MA), and NH4Cl. Results indicated AACRNLβ‘s interference with TRAF6 expression is ubiquitin-dependent (Fig. 7f). Next, we investigated the effect of AACRNLβ on the ubiquitination modification of TRAF6. AACRNLβ knockdown inhibited, while overexpression promoted, TRAF6 ubiquitination, which depended on AACRNLβ’s ADP-ribosylation activity (Fig. 7g, h). AACRNLβ overexpression significantly inhibited K27-, K33-, K48-, and K63-linked polyubiquitination of TRAF6 compared to other types of linkage (Fig. 7i, Supplementary Fig. 2a), and this regulation required AACRNLβ‘s ADP-ribosylation activity (Fig. 7j, k, Supplementary Fig. 2b, c). Given that TRAF6-mediated K27-linked ubiquitination of TAK1, and K63-linked ubiquitination of TBK1 or NEMO are crucial for responding to pathogenic infections20–22, AACRNLβ inhibits this ubiquitination activity through its ADP-ribosylation activity, thereby suppressing the immune signaling (Fig. 7l–n). These results suggest that AACRNLβ induces mono-ADP-ribosylation of TRAF6, facilitating its ubiquitin–proteasome–dependent degradation and impairing its function as a central E3 ligase in immune signaling, thereby contributing to toxicity and selfish reproduction.

TRAF6 ubiquitinates and degrades AACRNLβ as an antidote
As AACRNLβ remains toxic in the host, the host may implement counteracting detoxification functions to sustain immune equilibrium. Upon exposure to MG132, 3-MA, NH4Cl, and CQ, only MG132—a 26S proteasome inhibitor—significantly elevated AACRNLβ protein expression, indicating that the ubiquitin-proteasome system likely serves as a detoxifying pathway for AACRNLβ (Fig. 8a). Our research suggests that AACRNLβ, derived from AACRN effector, can inhibit the E3 activity of TRAF6. We then explored whether TRAF6 could use its ubiquitination activity to degrade AACRNLβ and act as an antidote. Results showed that knockdown or overexpression of TRAF6 increased or decreased AACRNLβ protein levels, supporting our hypothesis (Fig. 8b, c). Transfection of TRAF6 or its truncated mutants in MKC cells revealed that the TRAF6ΔRing and TRAF6ΔZF mutants, which lack E3 activity, could not degrade AACRNLβ (Fig. 8d). This degradation was independent of binding interactions since both TRAF6 and its mutants still interacted with AACRNLβ (Fig. 8e). Additionally, knockdown or overexpression of TRAF6 significantly reduced or enhanced the K48 ubiquitin modification of AACRNLβ (Fig. 8f, g). These findings suggest that TRAF6 can degrade AACRNLβ to counteract its inhibition, and serve as an antidote in the host’s body.

## Methods

Identification of AACRN(L) proteins in organisms
BLASTP and TBLASTN searches were conducted on the NCBI database (https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Blast.cgi), and target sequences with e-values above 10−10 and proteins with unrelated domain were discarded. These target sequences were used to perform iterative-BLAST to find more AACRN(L) proteins in eumycota and animalia.

Alignment, phylogenetic, and synteny analysis
Protein and DNA sequences were aligned by MUSCLE software (v3.8.31) for its high accuracy and speed, and Jalview software (v2.10) is used for visualizing comparison results. Maximum likelihood (ML) phylogenetic trees were generated using MEGA7, with WAG+G model and 1000 bootstrap replicates. Neighbor-Joining (NJ) trees were generated using MEGA7, with JTT model and 1000 bootstrap replicates. ITOL website (https://itol.embl.de/) were used to beautify the above phylogenetic tree. For gene synteny analysis, AACRNL genes were used as focal reference gene to TBLASTN the genome of seven indicated fish (S. Formosus, M. miiuy, P. platessa, O. latipes, O. niloticus, A. alosa, and D. rerio).

Domain, tertiary structure, and molecular docking analysis
The protein domain structure was predicted by the SMART website (http://smart.embl-heidelberg.de/). The tertiary structure of AACRNL proteins were predicted by AlphaFold Server (https://golgi.sandbox.google.com/). The molecular docking between mART domains and NAD+ were performed by AlphaFold Server website (AlphaFold Server (google.com)) and PyMOL software.

Identification of transposable elements flanking the AACRNL gene
To investigate the replicative transposition mechanism of AACRNL, ~5 kb of genomic DNA flanking the AACRNL gene was extracted. Then we used the BLAST tool at FishTEDB (https://www.fishtedb.com/) and Dfam website (https://dfam.org/search/sequence) to analyze potential transposon components.

Fish and challenge
M. miiuy (~50 g) was obtained from Zhoushan Fisheries Research Institute, Zhejiang Province, China. Fish was acclimated in aerated seawater tanks at 25°C for 6 weeks before experiments. In the SCRV injection group, fish was challenged with 200 μl SCRV at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 5 through intraperitoneal. As a comparison, 200 μl of physiological saline was used to challenge the individuals. Afterwards, the fish were sacrificed at different time points, and kidney and spleen tissues were collected for RNA extraction. SCRV virus was isolated as described previously39.

Cell culture
M. miiuy kidney cells (MKCs) were cultured in L-15 medium (HyClone) supplemented with 15% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Gibco), 100 U/ml penicillin, and 100 μg/ml streptomycin at 26°C. MKC cells were prepared from the kidney of M. miiuy as previously described40. EPC cells (ATCC, RRID: CVCL_4361) were maintained in medium 199 (HyClone) supplemented with 10% FBS (Gibco), 2 mM of L-glutamine, 100 U/mL of penicillin, and 100 mg/mL of streptomycin under humidified conditions at 26°C with 5% CO2. HEK293T cells (ATCC, RRID: CVCL_0063) were cultured in DMEM (HyClone) supplemented with 10% FBS, 100 U/ml penicillin, and 100 mg/ml streptomycin at 37°C in 5% CO2. All cells were tested negative for mycoplasma contamination and morphologically confirmed. No cell line was used for more than 20 passages after thawing from frozen stocks.

Cells transfection
Cells were transiently transfected with siRNA in 24-well plates using Lipofectamine RNAiMAX (Invitrogen) and with DNA plasmids using Lipofectamine 3000 (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. For functional analyses, the overexpression plasmid (500 ng per well) and siRNA (100 nM) were transfected into cells in a culture medium and then harvested for further detection.

RNA interference
The AACRNLβ-specific small interfering RNA (siRNA; si-AACRNLβ-1 and si-AACRNLβ-2) sequences were 5′-GGAUGUUUCAACAAGAUCATT-3′ and 5′-GGACUUCUGUUGAAAGAAATT-3′, respectively. The TRAF6-specific small interfering RNA (si-TRAF6) is as follows: 5′-ACACCAUGCAAGGAGCUUUTT-3′. The scrambled control RNA sequences were 5′-UUCUCCGAACGUGUCACGUTT-3′.

Plasmids construction
The full-length coding sequence (CDS) of expression proteins of miiuy croaker (M. miiuy) were generated by PCR and cloned into pcDNA3.1 (Invitrogen) with specific tags. HA-tagged wild-type ubiquitin (UB-HA) and HA-tagged ubiquitin mutant expression plasmids were constructed with the template of pRK5-HA-ubiquitin-WT (Addgene, Cat# 17608) using ClonExpress II One Step Cloning Kit (Vazyme). Site or deletion mutants of AACRNLβ and TRAF6 were amplified by PCR with specific primers based on the recombinant plasmid. For protein purification, expression plasmids with 8× His tag was constructed based on pcDNA3.1. The correct construction of the recombinant plasmids was verified through Sanger sequencing and extracted using an Endotoxin-Free Plasmid DNA Miniprep Kit (Tiangen, China). The primers are listed in Supplementary Data 1.

Cell viability
Cell viability was assessed 48 h post-transfection in MKCs using the Cell-Titer-Glo luminescent assay (Promega), following the manufacturer’s protocol.

Protein purification and analysis
(His8)-tagged expression plasmids of M. miiuy were transiently overexpressed in 293T cells and lysed in a binding buffer (500 mM NaCl, 20 mM Tris/HCl [pH 7.4], 20 mM Imidazole, and 1% Triton X-100) including protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche). The lysate was incubated overnight at 4°C with anti-His beads (Solarbio). Anti-His beads were washed subsequently with washing buffer (500 mM NaCl, 20 mM Tris/HCl [pH 7.4], 20 mM Imidazole, and 1% Triton X-100). Proteins were eluted by addition of elution buffer (500 mM NaCl, 20 mM Tris/HCl [pH 7.4], 500 mM Imidazole, and 1% Triton X-100) to the beads. The purity of recombinant proteins was determined by SDS-PAGE separation or ponceau S. The purified AACRNLβ and AACRNLβ-HYY proteins were used to perform in vitro ADP-ribosylation assays.

RNA extraction and quantitative real-time PCR
The TRIzol Reagent (Invitrogen) was utilized for total RNA extraction, and subsequent cDNA synthesis was performed using the FastQuant RT Kit (Tiangen). The expression profiles of each gene were conducted by using the SYBR Premix Ex Taq™ (Takara). Quantitative real-time PCR was carried out using an Applied Biosystems® QuantStudio 3 (Thermo Fisher Scientific). β-actin served as the internal control for mRNA. The primer sequences are detailed in Supplementary Data 1.

Western blotting
Cellular lysates were prepared using 1× SDS-PAGE loading buffer. Protein extraction from cells was conducted, and quantification was performed using the BCA Protein Assay kit (Vazyme). The proteins were separated by SDS-PAGE (10%) and transferred onto PVDF membranes using a semidry blotting technique (Bio-Rad Trans Blot Turbo System). The membranes were then blocked with 5% BSA and probed with various antibodies. The antibody against AACRNLβ was diluted at 1:1000 (Customized in Genscript); The antibody against TRAF6 was diluted at 1: 500 (Boster, A00185); The antibody against IκBα was diluted at 1:500 (absin, abs106057); The antibody against TNF-α was diluted at 1:500 (ABclonal); The antibody against H3K27me3 (Beyotime, AF5710), H3K9me3 (Beyotime, AF5707), H3 (Beyotime, AF7101), and EZH2 (Beyotime, AF6828) were diluted at 1:500 (Beyotime); anti-Flag (Beyotime, AF519), anti-Myc (Beyotime, AF2864), anti-HA (Beyotime, AH158) and anti-Tubulin (Beyotime, AT819) monoclonal antibodies were diluted at 1: 1000; and HRP-conjugated anti-rabbit IgG (Abbkine, A25022) or anti-mouse IgG (Abbkine, A25012) at 1:5000. The immunoreactive proteins were visualized using Western Bright TM ECL (Advansta), and digital imaging was conducted with a cold CCD camera.

Co-immunoprecipitation
The cells were lysed in the cold IP buffer. The supernatant from cell lysates was incubated with indicated antibodies. Then, the protein A/G beads were incubated with the lysates overnight at 4°C. The beads were washed three times with cold lysis buffer and resuspended in the protein loading buffer. The immunoprecipitates and whole-cell lysates were followed by western blotting analysis.

Ni2+-NTA pull-down assay
Ni2+-NTA pull-down assay was done as described previously41. Cells cultured in 10-cm plates were transfected with the indicated plasmids. Cells from each plate were washed and collected with ice-cold PBS and divided into two aliquots. One sample was lysed with NP-40 lysis buffer and analyzed by immunoblotting directly to examine the expression of indicated proteins. Another sample was lysed in buffer A (8 M urea, 50 mM NaHPO4.H2O, 300 mM NaCl, 10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 10 mM imidazole) and subjected to sonication for 20 s. Cell lysates were incubated with 50-µL pre-equilibrated Ni2+-NTA beads (denaturation type) for 8 h at 4°C. Then, beads were washed four times sequentially with buffer A and B (same as A except with 20 mM imidazole). Beads bound with His-tagged proteins were boiled with 2× SDS loading buffer containing 200 mM imidazole and were subjected to immunoblot.

Immunofluorescence
Cells cultured on glass coverslips in 24-well plates were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min following a triple wash with PBS. The cells were permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100 in PBS (PBST) for 15 min. After a 60-min block with 5% BSA, the cells were subjected to a 10-h incubation with the primary antibody at 4°C. Following three washes with PBS, the cells were exposed to a fluorescent-dye conjugated secondary antibody for 60 min at room temperature. Post a 10-min DAPI counterstain, the fluorescence signals of the cells were captured using a Leica fluorescence microscope.

In vitro ADP-ribosylation assay
After obtaining the purified proteins, ADP-ribosylation assays were carried out in 30-ml reaction buffer (50 mM Tris, pH 8.0, 0.2 mM DTT, 4 mM MgCl2) with 100 mM NAD+ (Macklin, N814818) or 100 mM Bio-NAD+ (Mreda, M256875) for 45 min at room temperature. The reactions were stopped by addition of SDS sample buffer, and the products were probed with mono-ADP-Ribose antibody (BIO-RAD, AbD33204) or streptavidin–HRP (Beyotime, A0303).

In vivo ADP-ribosylation analysis
MKC cells were transfected with AACRNLβ-Myc or AACRNLβ-HYY-Myc plasmids, then cell lysate was immunoprecipitated by Myc antibody and the interacted proteins with mono-ADPr modification were immunoblotted with mono-ADPr antibody to analyse the ADP-ribosylation effects of AACRNLβ in vivo. To detect whether TRAF6 and EZH2 have mono-ADPr modification in vivo, MKC cell lysate was immunoprecipitated by IgG antibody or mono-ADP-Ribose antibody, then TRAF6 and EZH2 antibody were used to detect mono-ADP-ribosylation.

Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay
MKC cells were seeded in 10 cm² dishes and transfected with plasmids once the cell density reached 5.0 × 10⁶. For chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP), cells were cross-linked with 1% formaldehyde at 37°C for 10 min, then quenched with glycine for 5 min at room temperature. After two washes with PBS, cells were lysed on ice, collected, and sonicated to shear chromatin. Lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 12,000 rpm (~13,800 × g) for 10 min at 4°C. The resulting supernatant was incubated with the appropriate antibody overnight at 4°C with rotation. Protein A/G agarose beads were added and incubated for 2 h at 4°C. After centrifugation at 6000 rpm (~3500 × g) for 5 min, the supernatant was discarded. Beads were sequentially washed with low-salt wash buffer (twice), LiCl wash buffer, and TE buffer. Immunocomplexes were eluted with elution buffer and diluted to 500 ml using diffusion buffer. Cross-links were reversed by adding 5 M NaCl and incubating at 65°C for 12 h, followed by treatment with 0.5 M EDTA, 1 M Tris-HCl, and 20 mg/ml Proteinase K at 45°C for 2 h.

Statistical analysis
Statistical analyses were performed using Prism v8 (GraphPad Software). Data are expressed as the mean ± SE from at least three independent experiments, each performed with three technical replicates. Comparisons between two groups were performed using a two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test. For comparisons involving more than two groups, one-way ANOVA followed by Duncan’s post-hoc multiple comparison test was conducted. The relative gene expression data was acquired using the 2−ΔΔCT method42. Effect sizes (Cohen’s d for t-tests and η² for ANOVA) were calculated within Prism v8. A value of p < 0.05 was considered significant.

Ethics statement
All animal experimental procedures were performed in accordance with the National Institutes of Health’s Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals, and the experimental protocols were approved by the Research Ethics Committee of Shanghai Ocean University (No. SHOU-DW-2025-033).

In this manuscript, the discovery of a ‘selfish’ gene product that is endemic to a variety of organisms within multiple phyla is reported. The authors describe AACRN as a Crinkler family protein product encoded in host genomes that resembles pathogenic gene products. The authors go on to characterize the genetic structure of AACRN families and conclude that beta and gamma members in fish species are preferentially replicating themselves within their hosts genome. They elucidate that AACRN is often within a non-autonomously replicating transposon and that AACRN is able to interact with EZH2 to inhibit histone methylation of the transposon and thereby increase their expression and subsequent ability to propagate with the transposon. Given that these types of pathogenic gene products and transposition mechanisms activate host immune mechanisms the authors investigated how AACRN manipulates host defense mechanisms. To this end they describe how AACRN can ADP ribosylate TRAF6 and target it for ubiquitylation and degradation.
Overall, this is a well written and intriguing body of work describing a novel form of selfish gene or pathogenic gene product that has persisted in host genomes. I have a few suggests of places to improve the manuscript before publication. They are ranked roughly in order of importance for improving the manuscript.

## Paper

## Abstract

Crinkler effectors are iconic toxins deployed by pathogens to suppress host immunity, a function long thought exclusive to pathogenic species. Here, we uncover a striking evolutionary twist: an ADP-ribosyltransferase-associated Crinkler-like protein that has repurposed its toxin-derived activity to function as an epigenetic parasite in free-living eukaryotes, challenging the paradigm that Crinkler effectors are exclusively pathogen-restricted virulence factors. The ADP-ribosyltransferase-associated Crinkler-like protein retains a functional mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase domain homologous to diphtheria toxin, yet exhibits degeneration of N-terminal host-targeting domain, severing ties to canonical pathogenic functions. This activity enables dual subversion of host mechanisms: the ADP-ribosyltransferase-associated Crinkler-like protein mono-ADP-ribosylates the EZH2, reducing H3K27me3-mediated silencing and reactivating its own locus and adjacent transposons to drive replicative amplification; simultaneously, it modifies the immune adaptor TRAF6, suppressing NF-κB and IRF3 pathways to weaken innate immune surveillance and facilitate sustained propagation within the host genome. Notably, this parasitic strategy is countered by host detoxification: TRAF6 ubiquitinates ADP-ribosyltransferase-associated Crinkler-like protein, targeting it for proteasomal degradation. Together, our findings reveal how a toxin-derived effector escaped pathogenic contexts to evolve as a selfish genomic element, leveraging toxin-like activity to subvert epigenetic and immune barriers and redefining the evolutionary potential of Crinkler toxins as drivers of genomic conflict beyond pathogenicity.

## Introduction

Pathogenic microbes rely on secreted effector proteins to commandeer host cells and facilitate infection1,2. These virulence factors can disable immune defenses, hijack signaling pathways, and reprogram host physiology to the pathogen’s advantage1,2. In Gram-negative bacteria, type III secretion system effectors are renowned for targeting mitochondria and other organelles to control host cell death and inflammation3. Among oomycetes and fungi, Crinkler (CRN) proteins constitute a prominent effector family that exemplifies the complexity of host manipulation strategies4. First discovered in the potato late blight pathogen Phytophthora infestans, certain CRNs induced a characteristic leaf “crinkling and necrosis” phenotype when expressed in plants, highlighting their virulence potential5.

Structurally, canonical CRN effectors exhibit a modular architecture comprising conserved N-terminal and C-terminal domains that underpin their functional versatility6. The N-terminal domain, ~130 amino acids in length, includes the LXLFLAK motif, ubiquitin-like (UBL) folds, and α-helical structures responsible for host cell translocation4,7. The C-terminal region of CRN encompasses several effector functionalities, including restriction endonuclease (REase), protein kinase, HNH endonuclease, LK nuclease (a RNase), and multiple distinct peptidase domains, predicted to carry their toxicity determinants4,6,8,9. This modularity is thought to enable CRNs to diversify rapidly in response to selective pressures, fueling pathogen adaptation during host-pathogen coevolution.

Unexpectedly, recent comparative genomics surveys have uncovered CRN homologues across multiple free-living eukaryotic lineages, including chlorophyte algae, land plants, amoebozoans, and animals, challenging the long-held notion that these effectors are exclusive to pathogenic taxa7. This unexpected distribution raises fundamental questions about their evolutionary persistence: why do such virulence-associated genes remain embedded in the genomes of non-pathogenic organisms, and what functions, if any, do they perform outside classical pathogenic contexts? Addressing these questions is essential to expanding our understanding of effector evolution and function beyond classical pathogen-host paradigms.

Effector genes often reside within dynamic genomic contexts shaped by transposable elements and mobile genetic elements that facilitate their mobilization and diversification in pathogens10. Such genes are typically subject to strong positive selection because their toxin functions confer clear fitness benefits during infection, facilitating immune suppression and colonization11. By contrast, free-living non-pathogenic eukaryotes are ecologically isolated, limiting horizontal gene transfer opportunities through plasmids, viruses, or symbiotic interactions, which constrains the spread of virulence-associated genes. Furthermore, these sequences are often targets of host epigenetic repression mechanisms—such as H3K27me3-mediated chromatin silencing and DNA methylation—that restrict expression and genomic propagation of potentially invasive elements12,13. These constraints have reinforced the paradigm that effectors are confined to pathogenic contexts and rendered their evolutionary persistence in nonpathogenic genomes largely enigmatic.

Here, we report the discovery and functional characterization of a CRN homologue, ADP-ribosyltransferase-associated CRN-like (AACRNL), whose homologues are broadly distributed across free-living eukaryotic lineages. Unlike canonical CRNs, AACRNL have retained functional toxin-like enzymatic module but exhibit degeneration of N-terminal targeting domain, uncoupling them from classical host translocation. Remarkably, AACRNL co-opts its ART activity to mono-ADP-ribosylate EZH2, eroding H3K27me3-dependent repression and enabling the activation and replication of its own locus and adjacent transposons. Concurrently, AACRNL modifies TRAF6 to suppress NF-κB/IRF3 signaling, creating an immunologically permissive environment for its expansion. This dual strategy reveals how a virulence-derived effector can be repurposed as an epigenetic parasite in free-living eukaryotes, challenging conventional views of CRN biology and illuminating broader principles of genome conflict and adaptation.

## Results

Distribution and degeneration of AACRN(L) in free-living eukaryotes
The canonical CRN effector consists of an N-terminal domain responsible for host targeting and a toxin-related C-terminal domain (Fig. 1a). Based on this modular architecture, we identified a distinct type of CRN effectors, termed AACRN, characterized by an N-terminal UBL domain and a C-terminal ADP-ribosyltransferase (ART) domain (Fig. 1b). In addition, we identified a related variant in which the UBL domain has undergone extensive degeneration; we refer to this lineage as AACRN-Like (AACRNL) (Fig. 1b). Although AACRN effectors are typically associated with pathogenic functions, AACRN(L) homologs are also present in several free-living eukaryotes. Specifically, comprehensive search across multiple phyla revealed that the AACRN(L) family were detected in free-living eukaryotes like Porifera, Cnidaria, Echinodermata, Chordata, Rotifera, Nematora, and Arthropoda of animalia (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Fig. 1). Notably, the occurrence of AACRN(L) genes is limited to a minority of taxa and can vary considerably even within the same phylum. For example, within Chordata, the AACRNL family was identified exclusively in Actinopteri, a class of bony fish, which is also the highest living organism distributed by the AACRNL family (Fig. 1c). Given that the N-terminal domain is critical for host targeting, we examined its integrity in these free-living organisms. We observed pronounced degeneration of the N-terminal regions in AACRN effectors. For instance, the AACRNL homologues from Acipenser ruthenus and Porites lobata, the UBL domain has degenerated and lost the essential RGG motif required for ubiquitin chain formation (Fig. 1d, e). Overall, these findings demonstrate that AACRNL homologues persist in the genomes of certain free-living eukaryotes, and their N-terminal domain responsible for host targeting has also degraded, which may reflect a potential functional shift.

AACRNL exerts toxicity in free-living organisms through its ADP-ribosyltransferase activity
To identify the key residues responsible for the ADP-ribosyltransferase activity of AACRN(L), we collected AACRN(L) protein sequences from different phyla, along with two well-characterized bacterial toxins with mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase (mART) activity: diphtheria toxin from Corynebacterium diphtheriae and exotoxin A from Pseudomonas aeruginosa14. Sequence alignment of the mART domain revealed a conserved H-Y-Y motif (Fig. 2a), which is essential for NAD⁺ co-substrate binding15. Next, we extracted the structural domain sequences of Miichthys miiuy AACRNL and C. diphtheriae diphtheria toxin, performing molecular docking with NAD+. The results showed that in both AACRNL and diphtheria toxin, both the “H” and the “Y” residues had interatomic contacts with NAD+ (Fig. 2b). To validate the functional importance of this motif, we generated point mutations in the H-Y-Y motif of M. miiuy AACRNL (Fig. 2c). AACRNL efficiently co-precipitated mono-ADP-ribosylation (mono-ADPr) from cell lysates, but AACRNL-HYY mutants did not (Fig. 2d). Additionally, self-modifying activity tests showed that AACRNL, but not AACRNL-HYY, was modified by mono-ADP-ribose (Fig. 2e). Furthermore, when purified AACRNL or AACRNL-HYY proteins were incubated with biotin-labeled NAD+, only AACRNL’s auto-modification was detected by streptavidin-HRP on western blots (Fig. 2f). Considering the structural homology between AACRNL and diphtheria toxin, as well as the origin of its toxin effector domain, we further investigated whether AACRNL functions as a toxin in fish, the highest-order lineage where AACRNL is distributed. Indeed, we found that AACRNL exerts mART-dependent inhibition of cellular viability (Fig. 2g). In addition, AACRNL suppressed the IRF3 and NF-κB pathways and downregulated the expression of antiviral and pro-inflammatory factors (Fig. 2h–k). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that AACRNL possesses robust mART activity and retains toxin-like functions even in free-living eukaryotes.

AACRNL replicates in teleost via adjacent transposable elements
We further assessed the distribution and abundance of AACRNL genes in teleost, the highest-level vertebrate group in which AACRNL homologs have been identified so far. AACRNL exhibits lineage-specific expansion and contraction in bony fish, with Cyprinus carpio displaying the highest number of AACRNL copies, although their transcriptional activity is yet to be elucidated (Fig. 3a). In contrast, Takifugu rubripes is the only bony fish lacking AACRNL (Fig. 3a). Through a comprehensive analysis of chromosome-level whole genome data from seven fish species (Scleropages Formosus, M. miiuy, Pleuronectes platessa, Oryzias latipes, Oreochromis niloticus, Alosa alosa, and Danio rerio), we found that phylogenetic analysis of AACRNLs from these fish species revealed significant clustering into three lineages, which we refer to as AACRNLα, AACRNLβ, and AACRNLγ (Fig. 3b). The linear relationship around the AACRNLα gene is relatively conservative and single copy, indicating that it has lost its replication ability (Fig. 3b, c). However, AACRNLβ and AACRNLγ exhibit a very limited linear relationship and multiple copies, indicating that they have undergone replication (Fig. 3b, c).

To investigate the replication mechanisms of AACRNLβ and AACRNLγ, we examined their surrounding genomic sequences. Among the three copies identified in M. miiuy, AACRNLα was unable to transpose, while the other two included AACRNLβ and another copy that had become inactive, which we designated pAACRNLβ (Fig. 3c). Based on their linear arrangement, the right flank of pAACRNLβ was identical to that of AACRNLβ, both containing the hce1 and lce1 genes, indicating that pAACRNLβ originated from the duplication of AACRNLβ (Fig. 3d). Notably, we observed terminal inverted repeats (TIRs) of a non-autonomous hAT_Charlie transposable element flanking both sides of the AACRNLβ and lce1 loci, suggesting that the replication and transposition of AACRNLβ may have been mediated by the hAT_Charlie (Fig. 3d). We also found that autonomous mariner transposon elements are present on both sides of the AACRNLβ1 and AACRNLβ3 genes in P. platessa. Upstream of AACRNLβ1, there is the gtse1 gene, and within the last intron, the 5′ TIR and transposase of an autonomous mariner transposon are present. At the 3′ flanking region of AACRNLβ3, the 3′ TIR of an autonomous mariner transposon is detected. Analysis of the flanking regions of the AACRNLβ4, AACRNLβ5, and AACRNLβ6 genes in P. platessa also revealed autonomous mariner transposon elements together with the last exon of gtse1, confirming that these genes indeed originated through transpositional duplication from AACRNLβ1, AACRNLβ3, and related loci (Fig. 3e). Similarly, TIR sequences of non-autonomous hAT transposons were also detected flanking the AACRNLγ1 locus in zebrafish, further supporting our hypothesis (Fig. 3f). In summary, our research found that AACRNL can rely on neighboring transposable elements for selfish propagation in teleost genomes.

AACRNLβ abrogates H3K27me3-dependent repression of its locus and flanking hAT elements
Given that transposable elements in the host genome are generally maintained in a silenced state, yet replicative transposition of AACRNL is remarkably prevalent, this suggests that AACRNL may possess the capacity to activate these elements. Sequence alignment of the conserved “HGT” motif, which is essential for mART activity15, revealed that AACRNLα has lost this enzymatic function, whereas AACRNLβ and AACRNLγ retain intact catalytic domains (Fig. 4a). Consistent with their mobility, AACRNLα was unable to undergo replication, whereas AACRNLβ and AACRNLγ exhibited active transposition (Fig. 3b–f). These observations suggested that the intrinsic mART activity of AACRNL might be required for its selfish propagation (Fig. 4a). H3K27me3 and H3K9me3 are key chromatin modifications that silence transposable elements and repress gene transcription16. We found that M. miiuy AACRNLα, which lacks mART activity, was unable to suppress H3K27me3 levels, whereas AACRNLβ effectively reduced this repressive mark (Fig. 4b). Consistently, the AACRNLβ-HYY mutant, which has lost mART activity, also failed to inhibit H3K27me3 deposition (Fig. 4c). Given that H3K27me3 is deposited by the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2), we examined whether AACRNLβ interacts with PRC2 components. Co-immunoprecipitation experiments revealed that AACRNLβ specifically associated with EZH2, the catalytic subunit of PRC2, but not with SUZ12 (Fig. 4d). Moreover, immunoblotting with mono-ADP-ribose–specific antibodies confirmed in vivo mono-ADP-ribosylation of EZH2 (Fig. 4e). In vitro assays further demonstrated that AACRNLβ directly mediates mono-ADP-ribosylation of EZH2 (Fig. 4f, g). Beyond modifying EZH2, AACRNLβ also promotes the degradation of EZH2 protein in an enzymatic activity–dependent manner, without affecting ezh2 mRNA levels (Fig. 4h–j). Therefore, AACRNLβ can suppress H3K27me3 modification levels by inhibiting EZH2.

To determine whether AACRNLβ-driven reduction of H3K27me3 could relieve silencing at its own locus and neighboring hAT elements, we designed four pairs of ChIP-qPCR primers spanning the region from the AACRNLβ promoter to the 5′ TIR (Fig. 4k). Chromatin immunoprecipitation revealed that both AACRNLβ and the adjacent hAT sequences were enriched in H3K27me3 marks (Fig. 4l). Overexpression of EZH2 further increased H3K27me3 deposition, whereas co-transfection of wild-type AACRNLβ, but not the catalytically inactive mutant, effectively abrogated EZH2-mediated enrichment at these loci (Fig. 4m). Functionally, EZH2 suppressed AACRNLβ mRNA expression and decreased the recruitment of POLR2A, a core subunit of RNA polymerase II, to the AACRNLβ promoter (Fig. 4n, o). In contrast, co-transfection of AACRNLβ reversed this repression, suggesting that AACRNLβ is capable of self-activation (Fig. 4o). Consistently, siRNA knockdown of AACRN reduced POLR2A binding at its promoter (Fig. 4p). Collectively, these results demonstrate that AACRNLβ relieves H3K27me3-mediated silencing at its locus and neighboring hAT elements by targeting and modifying EZH2. This establishes a permissive chromatin environment that facilitates both self-activation and replicative transposition, thereby linking AACRNL’s mART enzymatic activity to its capacity for selfish genomic spread.

Viral infection triggers AACRNL activation and subsequent genomic instability
To investigate the activation dynamics and functional consequences of AACRNL, we analyzed its expression during zebrafish embryogenesis to capture baseline developmental activity, and upon viral infection to assess stress-induced activation. Single-cell analysis across early (4–6 h), mid (8–12 h), and late (24 h) embryonic stages showed that all five AACRNLγ members were transcriptionally silent, with AACRNLγ2, γ3, and γ5 loci enriched for H3K27me3, indicative of developmental repression (Fig. 5a). Notably, this silencing was reversible: SVCV infection strongly induced AACRNLγ2, γ3, and γ5, whereas γ1 and γ4 remained undetectable, suggesting potential loss of transcriptional competence in these loci (Fig. 5b). Similarly, M. miiuy AACRNLβ was markedly upregulated upon SCRV infection, as shown by RNA-seq and validated by qPCR in spleen, kidney, and MKC cells (Fig. 5c–f). Functional assays demonstrated that siRNA-mediated knockdown of AACRNLβ restored H3K27me3 levels suppressed by viral infection and prevented DNA damage, as indicated by tp53, p21, and gadd45a induction, revealing that infection-induced AACRNLβ promotes genomic instability (Fig. 5g, h). This function required AACRNLβ’s mART activity (Fig. 5i). Finally, wild-type AACRNLβ, but not the catalytically inactive AACRNLβ-HYY mutant, significantly increased the expression of transposon RNAs known to respond to pathogen challenge, including LINEs and ERVs (Fig. 5j). These findings indicate that pathogen-induced AACRNL activation promotes DNA damage and creates a permissive chromatin environment for transposon expression.

AACRNLβ mono-ADP-ribosylates TRAF6
Given that transposon activity and exogenous genetic elements often trigger host immune surveillance, we investigate how AACRNLβ creates an immune permissive environment to promote selfish reproduction. Co-immunoprecipitation results showed that AACRNLβ specifically binds to TRAF6, not to TRAF3, TBK1, TAK1, or NEMO proteins (Fig. 6a). Immunofluorescence revealed that AACRNLβ is in both the cytoplasm and nucleus, while TRAF6 is in the cytoplasm (Fig. 6b). Endogenous co-IP demonstrated that TRAF6 specifically interacts with AACRNLβ, and AACRNLβ and its mutants interact with TRAF6 with the same binding affinity (Fig. 6c, d). Mono-ADPr antibodies confirmed that TRAF6 undergoes mono-ribosylation in vivo (Fig. 6e), and AACRNLβ can mediate TRAF6 mono-ribosylation in vitro (Fig. 6f, g). To identify deribosylases that reverse this modification, we examined TRAF6-interacting proteins in our mass spectrometry data and discovered ARH3, a poly-ADP ribose glycohydrolase17,18. In addition, we also constructed a Macro-3 domain plasmid from the ARTD8 protein of M. miiuy responsible for specifically removing mono-ribosylation modifications18. His-pulldown results indicated that both ARH3 and Macro3 can interact with TRAF6 (Fig. 6h). Overexpression of AACRNLβ significantly promoted the binding of Macro3, but not ARH3, to TRAF6, while catalytically inactive AACRNLβ-HYY did not affect their interaction (Fig. 6i, j). These findings strongly support that AACRNLβ induces TRAF6 mono-ADP-ribosylation19.

AACRNLβ inhibits TRAF6-mediated ubiquitin signaling
To define how AACRNLβ-mediated mono-ADP-ribosylation affects TRAF6 function, we first examined its impact on TRAF6 stability. Knockdown or overexpression of AACRNLβ increased or decreased TRAF6 protein levels without affecting TRAF6 mRNA levels (Fig. 7a, b). During SCRV or V. anguillarum infection, AACRNLβ consistently suppressed TRAF6 protein expression (Fig. 7c). The AACRNLβ-HYY mutant also significantly degraded TRAF6, though less effectively (Fig. 7d). Cycloheximide (CHX) assays confirmed that AACRNLβ shortened the half-life of endogenous TRAF6 protein (Fig. 7e). To determine if AACRNLβ-mediated TRAF6 degradation was dependent on ubiquitin-proteasome, autophagosome, or lysosomal pathways, MKC cells were treated with MG132, 3-Methyladenine (3-MA), and NH4Cl. Results indicated AACRNLβ‘s interference with TRAF6 expression is ubiquitin-dependent (Fig. 7f). Next, we investigated the effect of AACRNLβ on the ubiquitination modification of TRAF6. AACRNLβ knockdown inhibited, while overexpression promoted, TRAF6 ubiquitination, which depended on AACRNLβ’s ADP-ribosylation activity (Fig. 7g, h). AACRNLβ overexpression significantly inhibited K27-, K33-, K48-, and K63-linked polyubiquitination of TRAF6 compared to other types of linkage (Fig. 7i, Supplementary Fig. 2a), and this regulation required AACRNLβ‘s ADP-ribosylation activity (Fig. 7j, k, Supplementary Fig. 2b, c). Given that TRAF6-mediated K27-linked ubiquitination of TAK1, and K63-linked ubiquitination of TBK1 or NEMO are crucial for responding to pathogenic infections20–22, AACRNLβ inhibits this ubiquitination activity through its ADP-ribosylation activity, thereby suppressing the immune signaling (Fig. 7l–n). These results suggest that AACRNLβ induces mono-ADP-ribosylation of TRAF6, facilitating its ubiquitin–proteasome–dependent degradation and impairing its function as a central E3 ligase in immune signaling, thereby contributing to toxicity and selfish reproduction.

TRAF6 ubiquitinates and degrades AACRNLβ as an antidote
As AACRNLβ remains toxic in the host, the host may implement counteracting detoxification functions to sustain immune equilibrium. Upon exposure to MG132, 3-MA, NH4Cl, and CQ, only MG132—a 26S proteasome inhibitor—significantly elevated AACRNLβ protein expression, indicating that the ubiquitin-proteasome system likely serves as a detoxifying pathway for AACRNLβ (Fig. 8a). Our research suggests that AACRNLβ, derived from AACRN effector, can inhibit the E3 activity of TRAF6. We then explored whether TRAF6 could use its ubiquitination activity to degrade AACRNLβ and act as an antidote. Results showed that knockdown or overexpression of TRAF6 increased or decreased AACRNLβ protein levels, supporting our hypothesis (Fig. 8b, c). Transfection of TRAF6 or its truncated mutants in MKC cells revealed that the TRAF6ΔRing and TRAF6ΔZF mutants, which lack E3 activity, could not degrade AACRNLβ (Fig. 8d). This degradation was independent of binding interactions since both TRAF6 and its mutants still interacted with AACRNLβ (Fig. 8e). Additionally, knockdown or overexpression of TRAF6 significantly reduced or enhanced the K48 ubiquitin modification of AACRNLβ (Fig. 8f, g). These findings suggest that TRAF6 can degrade AACRNLβ to counteract its inhibition, and serve as an antidote in the host’s body.
